selected.text: Barcodes failed because the longer start.

paragraphs.text: Barcodes failed because the longer start.

Start with the detail itself. Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate. They hold no number at all. On a UPC barcode, the start, middle and end guard bars extend lower. They encode no digit; they split the code into two halves. IBM's George Laurer was assigned to design a supermarket scanner label. His team defined guard bars so a scanner could detect the label. They even told it which half it was reading. So the longest bars are signposts, not data.

Its history begins with a practical problem. A UPC-A barcode has exactly 30 bars: 6 form guard patterns and 24 represent its 12 digits. IBM assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label. Splitting the label into two halves allowed the bars to be cut nearly in half in length.
That problem shaped the design. Laurer and a colleague defined guard bars and how a scanner should detect the label.

The documentation makes the purpose clearer. The governing physics: The longer start, middle and end guard bars encode no digit; they mark the label, split the digits and set the timing for the scanner. The start, middle and end guard bars of a UPC-A barcode extend further down than the digit bars. Guard patterns do not encode a digit; they help decoding. The guard patterns separate the two groups of six digits and establish the timing.

But one detail complicates the familiar story. Every stripe looks like data, but the longest bars carry no digit. The guard bars also identified which half of the label was being read and trained the scanner's threshold circuits.

The design did not stop changing there. A scanner can detect the label and tell which half it is reading. The first UPC-marked item scanned at a retail checkout was Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.
